summary: The 20 h milled sample is the powder of the non-equiatomic low-density high entropy steel Fe40Mn19Ni15Al15Si10C1 obtained after 20 h of high-energy mechanical alloying in a planetary ball mill — an intermediate milling state sampled from an XRD series (0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35 h) used to track the alloying behaviour of the elemental powder blend. At this stage alloying is well advanced (the intense Ni and Mn elemental reflections are no longer evident and Al had largely dissolved by 15 h) but a fully alloyed solid solution has not yet formed; average powder particle size is ~6 ± 2 µm. The research question addressed by the paper is how MA and subsequent spark plasma sintering control phase evolution, thermal stability, microstructure and mechanical properties of this low-density high entropy steel.
composition: Nominal composition Fe40Mn19Ni15Al15Si10C1 (at.%), i.e. Fe-46.00%, Mn-21.50%, Ni-18.13%, Al-8.34%, Si-5.78%, C-0.25% (wt.%). The alloy is a non-equiatomic, low-density high entropy steel built on an Fe-rich base with Mn, Ni, Al and Si as alloying additions and C as an interstitial element; the design intent is a low-density steel that develops a multiphase (mainly BCC + B2) microstructure with high strength and appreciable ductility. The starting charge consisted of elemental Fe, Ni, Mn, Al, Si and C powders of 99.2% purity taken in the above proportion. Elemental physicochemical data used to rationalise alloying are: atomic radii Fe 1.27, Mn 1.40, Ni 1.24, Al 1.40, Si 1.11, C 0.91 Å; densities Fe 7.87, Mn 7.4, Ni 8.91, Al 2.70, Si 2.3, C 2.1 g/cc; melting points Fe 1536, Mn 1244, Ni 1455, Al 660, Si 1414, C 3550 °C; self-diffusion coefficients Fe 10⁻³¹, Mn 10⁻³⁶, Ni 10⁻³⁶, Al 10⁻¹⁹, Si 10⁻⁶² m²/s (C not reported).
processing: Mechanical alloying (high-energy planetary ball milling) of the elemental powder blend for 20 h, carried out in a Retsch PM 400/2 planetary ball mill at 200 rpm with a ball-to-powder ratio of 10:1, using tungsten carbide vials and WC balls. Toluene was added as a process-control reagent to avoid oxidation during milling, and milling was interrupted for 20 min after every 1 h to prevent overheating. The 20 h state is a snapshot of a continuous milling campaign taken to 35 h, in which 2–3 g of powder was withdrawn after every 5 h to follow phase evolution; it is a precursor state to the 25–35 h milled powders that were subsequently annealed (400–800 °C) or consolidated by spark plasma sintering (900 °C, 50 MPa, 100 °C·min⁻¹, 15 min hold).
microstructure: At 20 h the powder is not yet a single-phase solid solution but an intermediate milling state. XRD shows that the low-intensity elemental peaks of all constituents had already vanished after 5 h and that Al has largely dissolved by 15 h; after 20 h the intense elemental peaks of Ni and Mn are no longer evident in the pattern, indicating that alloying of these two elements is well advanced. A fully alloyed structure consisting of BCC (a = 0.286 nm) plus γ-brass type (a = 0.872 nm) is only reported after 25 h of milling, so at 20 h the powder still contains residual elemental constituents. Particle morphology is finer and more fractured than at 10 h, with particles becoming progressively more homogeneous as milling continues; image analysis of SEM micrographs gives an average particle size of ~6 ± 2 µm (Gaussian fit, particle-size range about 1–11 µm, with a bimodal-looking distribution and a secondary bin near 3 µm), compared with ~10 ± 2 µm at 10 h, ~5 ± 1.5 µm at 30 h and ~4 ± 1 µm at 35 h. No quantitative grain size, texture or phase-fraction data are reported for this specific 20 h state.
properties: No mechanical, physical or functional property measurement is reported for the 20 h milled powder; the sample was characterised only microstructurally. The techniques applied to it are X-ray diffraction (EMPYREAN, PANALYTICAL, Co-Kα source, 40 kV, 40 mA, scan rate 5°·min⁻¹) as part of the milling-time series, scanning electron microscopy (Evo 18 Carl Zeiss SEM with EDS detector) to examine particle size, shape and morphology, and particle-size distribution analysis by image analysis (ImageJ) of the SEM micrographs. Mechanical properties (microhardness 7.8 ± 0.3 GPa, elastic modulus 184 ± 5 GPa, compressive strength 2046 ± 160 MPa, ~19% compressive ductility) and density (~6.49 ± 0.3 g cm⁻³) were obtained only on the SPSed pellet made from the 35 h milled powder, not on this intermediate powder.
mechanisms: Progressive alloying during milling: the diffraction intensity of the elemental peaks decreases with milling time, indicating that alloying is initiated early; low-intensity elemental peaks vanish after 5 h, Al largely dissolves by 15 h (highest alloying rate, attributed to its lowest melting point among the metallic constituents), and the intense Ni and Mn peaks disappear by 20 h, so that at this snapshot alloying of the major metallic elements is largely complete while a full solid solution is only reached at 25 h.

Dissolution sequence and kinetics: alloying is controlled by the physicochemical properties of the constituents — the diffusion of low-melting-point elements into the matrix of higher-melting-point elements governs the sequence (C dissolved fastest because of its small atomic size and high diffusivity, followed by Al, then Mn and Ni), with the rate dependent on melting point and self-diffusion coefficient; Si remains undissolved even after 35 h because of its lowest self-diffusion coefficient and non-metallic character.

Refinement and fragmentation mechanism: repeated fracturing and cold welding during high-energy milling continuously refine and fracture the powder particles, so that by 20 h the particles are markedly finer and more fractured than at 10 h and the powder becomes progressively more homogeneous as milling proceeds.

Peak broadening mechanism: the broadening and intensity loss of the diffraction peaks with milling arise from lattice distortion induced by atomic-size differences between the constituents, from mechanical deformation of the powder and from the increasing fraction of grain boundaries accompanying grain refinement.
conclusions: As a snapshot of the milling campaign, the 20 h milled powder establishes the intermediate stage of alloying in this low-density high entropy steel: alloying proceeds sequentially (C → Al → Mn, Ni), and only after 25 h of milling does a BCC (a = 0.286 nm) + γ-brass type (a = 0.872 nm) solid solution form, with the partially ordered B2-type phase appearing at 35 h. In the broader study this milling-time series underpins the phase-evolution picture of the alloy, whose metastable milled structure is thermally stable up to ~500 °C, transforms to Fe5Si3-type silicide from ~520 °C onwards, and after spark plasma sintering retains BCC as the major phase with B2 and trace γ-brass and Fe5Si3-type phases, giving a low density (~6.49 ± 0.3 g cm⁻³), high microhardness (7.8 ± 0.3 GPa) and high compressive strength (2046 ± 160 MPa) with ~19% ductility — properties attributed mainly to grain-boundary and dislocation strengthening, and which exceed those of conventional dual-phase/low-density steels and other reported HEAs.
unmapped: The 20 h milled powder is an intermediate state of the continuous milling campaign: powder was sampled (2–3 g) after every 5 h up to 35 h, and only the 35 h powder was subsequently annealed or consolidated by SPS.

For the 20 h state the powder particle-size histogram (Fig. 2(g)) spans about 1–11 µm with a fitted Gaussian average of ~6 ± 2 µm and an apparently bimodal distribution with a secondary bin near 3 µm; particle size was measured from SEM micrographs using ImageJ software.

At 20 h no contamination from the WC milling media was reported for the milling campaign (no WC signature was detected by X-ray energy dispersive spectroscopy, consistent with the authors' earlier work on WC-milled powders).

The melting point of the alloy calculated for this composition by a machine-learning approach and by the rule of mixture was 1638 K and 1620 K, respectively, part of the thermodynamic framework used to discuss phase formation in the alloy.
